corrections.critique: Strongest feature: Grayling precisely isolates the modal burden, explaining that mere logical compatibility between freedom and suffering cannot demonstrate that an omnipotent creator lacked access to a better free world. Principal limitation: His interrogative formulation does not independently establish feasible actualization, since counterfactuals of freedom or valuable goods might constrain which improved worlds are realizable. Live burden: The theistic defense must substantiate its stronger necessity claim, while Grayling still owes engagement with sophisticated feasibility accounts rather than relying exclusively on the intuitive describability of freedom without terrible natural evil. Locked score: This exceptionally relevant, logically disciplined, charitable reply decisively contacts the hidden premise and appropriately limits its conclusion, although its evidential warrant remains less complete than its forceful burden placement, supporting the locked very-strong score of 88.

Strongest feature: Grayling distinguishes the existence of morally sufficient reasons from having grounds to trust that such reasons explain tsunamis, childhood cancer, and gratuitous suffering. Principal limitation: His examples undermine claims that suffering benefits each victim, but do not fully exclude system-wide goods, benefits to others, prevention of worse outcomes, remote consequences, or independently grounded confidence in providence. Live burden: The defender must supply more than human ignorance to make divine care reasonable, while Grayling must address whether antecedent evidence for God could legitimately alter the evidential significance of otherwise inscrutable harms. Locked score: This coherent, centrally relevant, and charitable reply decisively contacts epistemic restraint and recompense, yet its incomplete treatment of broader unknown-reason strategies keeps evidential warrant below its strongest dimensions and supports the locked very-strong score of 88.
